utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Barney Thomas, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. Boris Zorko, Chad Mair, Alex Fielding, and Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Good afternoon, Mr. Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just to remind you, Mr. Vuksic, that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am aware of that, and I will abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Vuksic. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, before we start today, I'd like to enter into an agreement with you, if I could. When I ask you a question, if you could answer the question sometimes with a yes or no as succinctly and as briefly as possible, I'm sure that the Chamber and all the parties here would appreciate it. If you feel the need to explain an answer, of course, you'll have the opportunity to do so and you can ask, but sometimes the answers that you've given have gone into areas which are admittedly well within your purview of knowledge, and it's clear that you have a deep understanding and factual -- of the factual as well as conceptual information. But if you could be briefer, I think it would benefit us all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith, for this warning and for the words of recognition that you uttered. I believe that that was due to the form of the questions asked of me and it was almost impossible to answer them with a yes or a no. However, in the future, I will try to be brief and I would appreciate if you would direct me in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent the fault is mine, I do apologise and I'll try to correct that so that we are able to move ahead in an expeditious a manner as possible. Yesterday in your testimony you mentioned, I believe it was at page 12075, that is Muslim general was wounded during the departure of the JNA from Sarajevo. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, but now I can tell you his name. That was General Enes Taso.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to spend a moment on an issue that came to mind after you gave us that answer, which is, to your knowledge, could you tell us whether or not the Slovenian army during the war that you were discussing yesterday was comprised of former members of the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to some of the other republics which ultimately became states that you mentioned yesterday, I would ask you the same question, if you know. With regard to the army of Croatia, were the officers and soldiers of that army former members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you give us the same response, and by that I mean that the officers and soldiers of that army were former members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you the same answer, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Montenegro, would that be the same? Would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, only I would say that Montenegro didn't have its independent army at the time that we're talking about. It formed its own army only later, but in that army there are Serbs and members of other ethnic groups from the former Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And since you've mentioned the issue of Serbs and other ethnic groups, prior to the break-up of Yugoslavia, would it be fair to say that the army, that being the JNA, was a multi-ethnic army and the officers -- let me first of all ask you that question. Would it be fair to say that the army was a multi-ethnic army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a multi-ethnic army, and the primary task of the organ of the league of communists of Yugoslavia, then a single party state, was for it not to be only multi-ethnic but to have all members of all nationalities and national communities be proportionally represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that expansion of your answer. I think it does clarify. With regard to the leadership of these armies, each of the armies that we've now discussed, by that to make sure that we are together, the Croatian army, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and the Slovenian army, the leadership of each of those armies comprised of former JNA officers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were member of the Yugoslav People's Army, so both in the army and the leadership of Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina featured such members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe that we left off in your testimony actually in 1992, if we were to put a chronological time on it. And what I'd like to know very briefly is, from 1992, did your position change in the army with regard to your duties as being what I would call the contact person for western organisations and military attaches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from 1992 until the end of 1993, I was first with the JNA operations group for liaising with international organisations. That was a temporary organisation which later on became a permanent organisation and was renamed administration for liaisons with international organisations. In addition to changing the name of this organisation, my duties were also altered, not essentially, but just formally at first, I was deputy chief and then I was only assistant chief, although I continued to do the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. So your title changed, but your responsibilities remained the same; is that a fair recapitulation of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did the same job but my position was somewhat lower. A deputy is higher than an assistant, according to the rules in force at the time. Therefore, I was not promoted in the meantime, actually, I was demoted as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. And thereafter did you remain in that particular administration, that is the administration in which you were involved in the operations group for liaising with international operations, or did you move to another duty within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my own proposal, this organisational unit in which I was then was merged with the department for liaisons with international representatives. Towards the end of 1993, an administration was formed for liaising with foreign military representatives and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We can stop there for a moment. You say "at my own proposal," who was this proposal made to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, could you please turn off your mike.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presented this proposal to the Chief of General Staff, General Momcilo Perisic, while he visited the administration for liaising with international organisations. The reasons I stated was that all the duties relating to foreign affairs should be concentrated in one organisation alone and then that would be a more efficient and cost-effective way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it from the answer that you gave at line 23, which is an administration was formed for liaising with foreign military representatives and international organisations, that at that time General Perisic agreed with your proposal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the new responsibilities in that administration, that being liaising with foreign military representatives, did you have an increase in your title, were you promoted, did your position change, or did you maintain the same position within this new administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed head of this newly-formed administration. I was given a higher salary group equal to that of a general, but I didn't get the position of a general. Therefore, certain things in my status changed, but they were not significant changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us how long you remained in this position as head of the newly-formed administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in that position for exactly three years, that is to say until the end of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1997 when you ceased being the -- involved as the head in that particular administration, what were your duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at my request, my personal request, I was transferred -- or actually, I asked to be transferred to a different duty. A decision was then made that the best solution would be for me to be the military envoy accredited in West Germany, and then in the Netherlands. For that purpose, I was transferred to the intelligence administration of the General Staff in order to be prepared for assuming a new duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in this position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a military envoy from August 1998 until the 24th of March, 1999, when NATO-armed intervention against Yugoslavia began.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thereafter did you remain in the military or -- excuse me. And thereafter did you remain in the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After diplomatic relations were unilaterally severed between my government, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the USA, the UK, France, and the Federal Republic of Germany as a diplomat, I had to go back home. These relations were unilaterally severed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you went back home, you remained in the military for some period of time, I take it. What were your duties at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my return on the 27th of March, I reported to my superior and asked him what to do. I was told not to do anything, and to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After a period of waiting, were you then re-assigned to some new duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the bombing campaign stopped and the Kumanovo agreement was signed, which provided for the stoppage of the bombing, the Yugoslav Army and all other Yugoslav authorities withdrew from Kosovo, I contemplated my status because I was still not assigned any kind of duty. Therefore, I decided to do something that I had been pondering for a very long time before that, and that is to leave the army and not to have anything to do as an active-duty soldier in what had been happening in Yugoslavia for a long time. I asked for an immediate retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you retire from the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I filed my application on the 26th or 27th of July, 1999, and on that same day that application was published in the daily newspaper called "Blic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to interrupt. You we will get to that particular issue further down the line. Right now I'm just trying to get a chronological understanding of your employment history. I take it that you retired from the army in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I retired in early September 1999, and thereby my membership in the VJ ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you retired from the army in 1999, what did you occupy yourself with next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a retired army officer, or rather, a free citizen, which I should have been in any normal democratic country, I felt the need to become involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to become involved in politics, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what party did you become involved with in terms of your political endeavours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at the time General Perisic was also retired, he established a movement -- the movement for a democratic Serbia. We got together and we agreed that I should join his political party. Later on, this party became a member of the democratic opposition of Serbia which consisted of 18 political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your involvement in politics, were you or were you not elected to any offices as a member of this particular party, the movement for democratic Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although that was not my primary goal, I became a member of the Main Board and the Presidency of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you at any point elected to a national post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not even possible. Before the democratic opposition of Serbia took power we didn't have any kind of body, but one could say that it was the Presidency of the coalition of the 18 parties and the Presidency was made up of the chairman of these political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to -- could you tell us what -- what years you were involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was publicly and actively involved in politics as of September 1999, and it lasted until the fall of Milosevic's government, and beyond that, that is to say late 2000 and the beginning of 2001. In that capacity I was an MP in the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And while you were an MP in the national Republic of Serbia in late 2000 and the beginning of 2001, did you have occasion to have any conversations with any members of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning matters pending at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to meet a representative of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade, Mr. Dejan Mihov. This meeting took place at his initiative. He explained to me that certain individuals, representatives of the Tribunal, would like to talk to me and that they would explain the reasons for that. He asked me if I was willing to do that, and I said that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After that did you have occasion to meet with any members of the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met with representatives of the Tribunal, but I can't tell you their names nor their titles. We met -- I can't remember exactly, but I think in early 2001 in the Assembly building of the Republic of Serbia. And we talked for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you met in the Assembly building, that is the building where you had been -- where you served, where you had an office as a result of your involvement in the political party that you've spoken about; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we met in my office, in my capacity as a national delegate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- you said you met for two hours. Did you meet with these people once or twice or three times? Could you tell us how many times you met with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least once, I believe, that would be the most accurate answer. I'm not sure about any other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a result of the meeting that you had with these individuals, were you ever furnished with a copy of any statement or notes with regard to what transpired during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shouldn't you be asking the witness what happened in the meeting rather than telling him whether he was furnished with anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking if he was furnished with copies of what happened at the meeting, I'm not talking about what happened at the meeting, just if he was furnished with any information. With a copy. The only question is whether he was furnished with a copy of any statement or notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never met anyone from the ICTY again, nor indeed was I given any source of document whatsoever, and for that matter I did not sign anything at all that had to do with our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to this date, have you ever been supplied with any memorialisation in any form whatsoever the meeting which you had at your office at the parliament building concerning your contact with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I now wish to go back in time, and specifically back to 1993, and the subject matter that I'm going to be raising with you is specifically the subject matter of NordBat and the Pancevo barracks. And if I could -- first of all, could you explain to the Chamber, if you know, what does NordBat stand for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviation stands for the Nordic Battalion, as you have pointed out already. This was a mixed unit comprising members of the armies of Sweden, Finland, and Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you first become aware of NordBat or the Nordic Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the first time I came across NordBat was when the UN Security Council decided to dispatch peacekeeping forces to Macedonia. These were then called UNPREDEP, United Nations Preventive Forces. That was in the north of Macedonia, right next to the Yugoslav border, and that was where NordBat was deployed. I believe this was sometime in 1993. The next time I came across a peacekeeping unit called that was when NordBat came to the UNPROFOR base in Pancevo and stayed there for awhile. They were then supposed to be deployed somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. When the NordBat came to the UNPROFOR base in Pancevo, whose base was that, the Pancevo base?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR made a request at the Pancevo base to have a barracks made available to them for their use. As far as we understood, this was the logistics base of the UN peacekeeping forces, UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that UNPROFOR made a request to have barracks made available to them, who did they make that request to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR command followed a directive that had arrived from New York, whereupon the UNPROFOR command submitted a request to the federal government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after the request by UNPROFOR command was submitted to the federal government of Yugoslavia, do you know whether or not an agreement was entered into between UNPROFOR or any other international organisation and the federal government of Yugoslavia with regard to use of the Pancevo barracks for United Nations peacekeeping forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The request was given due consideration as a matter of regular procedure under such circumstances as prevailed at the time. There existed a federal body for relations with the peacekeeping forces and missions. The body was called federal committee. It was the federal committee for liaison or relations, I can't remember which it was, with peacekeeping forces and missions in the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was this federal committee part of the military or part of some other organ of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the federal committee was an organ of the federal government. It comprised specially appointed state officials or representatives from other government departments. Foreign affairs, defence, justice, interior, and so on and so forth. Therefore, the defence ministry, the General Staff in the Army of Yugoslavia were but one of the sectors that were to be represented in that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have up on the screen P372.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, if you would be so kind as to turn to your binder and go to tab number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that we may need to be in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. And I believe, Mr. Guy-Smith, that your opposite number does have a copy of the document that Mr. Vuksic is going to look at in his binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Most assuredly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he's had an opportunity to also look at the binder that Mr. Vuksic has been supplied with. And I don't think we have any of those kinds of difficulties, and if we do, I'm sure we'll be able to work them out during the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at this document, if you could, please, and I would like to direct your attention to paragraph number 1 initially, and then to paragraph number 3. Now, my question to you, sir, is first of all, were you aware of the fact that there was a meeting between General Cot, General Perisic, General Mladic, and General Novakovic in Belgrade on the 25th September, 1993? Excuse me, let me rephrase that. Were you aware of the fact that there were meetings between these gentlemen? My question was badly phrased.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this meeting at the time it was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to paragraph 3, the second sentence reads: "The contentious issue of the Pancevo barracks was also mentioned." And I'm wondering whether you can shed any light with regard to what the contentious issue was with regard to Pancevo barracks on the 25th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have some difficulty, Mr. Guy-Smith. The witness has just told us that he wasn't aware of these meetings. He obviously was not part of this meeting itself. How is he supposed to know what was being discussed in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's not -- I've asked the question a slightly different way. I'm asking him whether or not he was aware of a contentious issue with regard to Pancevo barracks. Whether or not he was at the meeting or not, he still could be aware of the contentious issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that a question that could have been asked even without showing him the document? If you show him the document and the document mentions a contentious issues then at least he must -- it is a specific issue that you want him to talk about, the one that is in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But if you just think that he may know of any contentious issue that surrounded the Pancevo barracks, that question can be put without the document being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, to the the extent that a contentious issue was discussed at this time I thought it would be of help and also it guides the witness and it limits and it focuses his testimony. That was my intent. I'm happy to ask more free-floating questions, but I think the consequences of that is self-evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But taking your position in mind, were you aware of the fact of there being any contentious issues at all with regard to Pancevo barracks in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Stop right there. Stop right there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the dispute concerning the Pancevo barracks being returned to the VJ by the international peacekeeping forces since the compound was leased to them to be used over a single year. The year was now out and I supposed General Perisic raised this contentious issue with the objective of having the compound returned to the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is the issue of having the compound returned to the VJ a matter that you discussed in your capacity with any members of international organisations, for example, UNPROFOR independent of what General Perisic may have done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was an issue that was raised several times during several talks that I had with all these representatives that you specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the discussion? What were the issues that were involved apart from the issue of returning the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem had two aspects to it. The first, whether Pancevo barracks should be returned or handed over. And the second, if UNPROFOR still needed a compound to be made available to them in Serbia or Belgrade, then we were to find another compound that we would allow them to use. This problem was successfully tackled at a later date. The other problem was that this compound that had been used by UNPROFOR for a year now had to be brought back to its original condition in order to be used as before. It is only natural that there was some wear and tear during the year the compound was being used by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it that at that point in time, and I'm asking the question in 1993 in the September, that that issue was resolved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first aspect was not something that was open to challenge. We believed it was our duty to make ourselves available to the UN peacekeeping forces because to begin with, they were there at the proposal of the previous Presidency of the SFRY, so you might say they had been invited by the Serbian side, under quotation marks simply because I'm at a loss for a better piece of phrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the second aspect, was that matter resolved then, since you said the first aspect was something not open to challenge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second aspect was also beyond dispute. There was some confusion at the outset. Some members of the VJ believed that this should be a textbook situation where someone was leasing a flat to someone else and now this other person was supposed to pay the rent. That's how they pictured the whole situation. And it took some time before the hotheads in the army understood that it was impossible to have relations like that with any peacekeeping missions or the UN, and that no rent such as we knew it would be paid. Nevertheless, they were, on the other hand, prepared to review or assess any damage that might have come about and look for a way to have some sort of indemnity paid to the VJ for any damage incurred. Once that had been understood, we took relatively little time finding a natural solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was payment ever made for the use of the Pancevo barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me stop you there. Can you tell us when payment was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't said payment was made. He says he does know whether payment --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He knows that for a fact [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please. Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Q. To your knowledge was payment ever made for the use of the Pancevo barracks? "A. I know that for a fact. "Q. Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know whether it was paid or not. The next question, logical question, is, was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it or was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best part of the payment or rather the highest amount that we received from the UN was a cheque written out to $900.000 brought to Belgrade by Mr. Kofi Annan in person, who at the time was assistant Secretary-General for peacekeeping operations. I'm not sure if I'm entirely right about his precise position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We can go out of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know who the cheque for $900.000 that was bought by Mr. Kofi Annan was delivered to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cheque was delivered to the administration of which I was then head. It was in our finance department that the cheque was received. Quite simply, by way of clarification, I was at the time a member of the Dayton delegation, so I wasn't physically in Belgrade at the time, and my deputy was acting on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if you were not physically in Belgrade at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Apologies to my learned friend, I'm not objecting, Your Honours. I just wonder if now that we are in open session the document can be taken off the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if you were not physically in Belgrade at the time, how did you become aware of the payment made by the United Nations to you for the use of the Pancevo barracks by the -- by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's pretty clear-cut. When the director of a company or the head of a department in the military comes back from somewhere, then his subordinates tend to inform him on anything of substance that may have happened over that period. The only thing I can say is that I was quite happy to be informed about that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That deals with one aspect of the issue in 1993, that being Pancevo barracks at one level, and the other aspect of the matter that we were going to be discussing was that of NordBat. Did there come a time in the fall of 1993 when you were contacted by anyone in the VJ concerning the NordBat Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "no," as you sit here today, do you recall if there were any problems as a result of the NordBat Battalion being in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you describe what those problems were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NordBat was not a problem in itself. Its arrival was not a problem and the time it spent there was no problem at all, well, not for awhile, that's understood. What was the problem then? The problem occurred at the logistics base of UNPROFOR at the Pancevo barracks. A total of 16 tanks and 34 APCs arrived there - I'm not sure about the figures - which caused quite a great amount of commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And why did this cause a great amount of commotion, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity as administration head and as a member of the federal committee for relations with international peacekeeping forces missions, and so on and so forth, I should have known about weapons of that calibre arriving anywhere in the territory of the FRY. Nevertheless, I did not get to know this through our regular procedure, rather, I was informed by an officer from my administration off the record. He simply happened to tell me, and I never heard about that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you were informed by an officer in your administration off the record, what do you mean by "off the record" here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't phrase that adequately. Each time a superior talks to one of his subordinates in an office, it's always official as long as they are talking about something that falls within the purview of that unit. Nevertheless, as I said, I should have been informed before the weapons ever turned up in Pancevo. Nevertheless, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you should have been informed before the weapons turned up in Pancevo, could you tell us who you should have been informed by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should have been informed of that through our regular channels at one of the sessions of the committee for relations with international peacekeeping forces and missions. However, that was not discussed at such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from receiving this information from a subordinate, did you have any further discussions with anyone within the VJ concerning the arrival of these particular weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next conversation was with General Momcilo Perisic, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please relate to us how that conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. One does not forget that easily. He called me via our red phone line, and I knew immediately who was on the other end. He asked me what I was doing and I told him well, I was -- I'm going about my tasks. And he said, well, it doesn't seem to be the case. Did you know that in Pancevo there are foreign tanks and APCs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you respond when he asked you that question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I responded to him by saying that officially I had not been informed, but that unofficially I was aware of it. He asked me to explain and I told him that I had not received anything through our official channels, through the federal committee, that is, but that I was told that by our liaison officer at the logistics base in Pancevo informed me of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that the end of the conversation then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic asked me if I was certain of that. I responded positively. And then he asked me whether I was aware of anyone in the VJ being aware of this or having considered this beforehand. I told him I had no such knowledge and that I was doubtful as to anyone from the VJ giving an approval for that given that no one had the authority to. He then responded by saying, well, are you aware that we now have a problem. And I said that I supposed as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What was the problem that you now had considering that these weapons were at the Pancevo barracks belonging to NordBat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was in ascertaining who gave approval, or rather, who was to blame for that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And above and beyond trying to determine responsibility for the event, did you discuss there being any other problems with regard to these particular weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that conversation, we did not discuss any other problems. However, given the fact that there were tanks and APCs in Pancevo, we concluded it by General Perisic asking me what we were to do next. I said that it was my proposal to ask for an inquiry to try to establish facts about who had given an approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the inquiry, do you know if such an inquiry was undergone -- I'm sorry, undertaken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the weapons themselves, do you know where those weapons were destined to go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was known that those weapons were supposed to be transported out of the FRY and into Bosnia-Herzegovina to be deployed in the Tuzla area. What does that mean? Well, I'm afraid I cannot tell you anything more precisely and I haven't pondered a lot about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the weapons being transported out of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and into the Bosnia-Herzegovina to be deployed in the Tuzla area, were the weapons going to be crossing any borders or boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The weapons had to cross what one could have referred to as the border between the FRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina, although it may not have been the case at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that crossing of that border, are you aware of there being any resistance on the other side to those weapons being transported to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The issue of the weapons and the territory of the FRY got a different dimension. It was no longer the question of what will happen with it, but also who was to blame for those weapons entering the territory of the FRY, but I am afraid that I cannot shed any further light as to the results of the inquiry. It was our conclusion that perhaps those weapons were to go in two different directions in order to leave the FRY. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Vuksic. Please try to listen to the question and try to answer the question as succinctly as you possibly can. The question is whether there was any resistance on the other side to those weapons being transported to Tuzla. Your answer is going to be yes there was, or no there was not, or I don't know, very short and concise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. You are correct. Yes, there was resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know where that resistance came from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That resistance came from Republika Srpska and its military and political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that issue to your knowledge, and by that I mean the deployment of NordBat and the movement of those weapons, ever resolved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Although I cannot tell you exactly when, however, I can tell you it happened within a reasonable amount of time, given that the military and political leadership of Republika Srpska finally gave their consent for the weapons to be transported into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I don't know whether that was supposed to take place in Republika Srpska itself, the area of Tuzla may and may not necessarily be within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated that it happened --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated that it happened within a reasonable amount of time. My last question to you with regard to this issue is, do you recall if that happened within the calendar year 1993 that this matter was resolved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to be moving on to another topic, Your Honours. I note the time. I suggest that we stop now as opposed to moving on it to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. We'll take a break now and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Between the times that we were referring to, that being September of 1993 and December of 1993, do you recall there being any other incidents of protest by UNPROFOR concerning matters that affected FRY, specifically the VJ and, I'm at this point referring to an incident at a bridge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what incident would that be, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident took place at a bridge close to Batina. Certain people stopped some international representatives and treated them improperly or roughly, at least that was the initial information I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go into -- I don't think we need to, actually. If you could pull up 27D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could go to your binder, sir, that would be tab number 8. We are waiting for something to be pulled up on the screen. Now, I'd like you to review the letter and, first of all, I would ask you, do you recognise this letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I do. I recognise the letter on the left-hand side of the screen since I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is this a letter that deals with the issue that you mentioned a moment before, that being of the Batina bridge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a letter of the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of VJ, which was drafted based on the letter I sent to the Chief of General Staff, or rather, to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we are clear, could you turn to tab 7 in your binder. Is that the letter that you wrote to the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think he was on the wrong tab, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in this letter, you indicate that in your opinion -- it says: "In our opinion, the protest is a means of putting pressure on the FRY in the spirit of Resolution 871 and this case could turn very serious if international factors think it necessary." Could you please explain to us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that a letter had arrived from UNPROFOR commander General Cot, it was of multiple significance. The VJ was asked to do something it could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was it being asked to do that it could not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was asked that we control in full the so-called border, and any movement of people between the then UN protected sector and the FRY. When I say "we" I mean the Army of Yugoslavia. This could have escalated in different ways. For example, General Cot, UNPROFOR commander, could assign greater or lesser importance to it, meaning in turn that in the UN or one might say in New York that case could cause more or less friction. Nothing before that time or after that, or at least very few things could have been unilaterally -- sorry, not unilaterally, unambiguously interpreted when borders were in question. And what were the tasks of what side and whether a particular side can meet a request especially within a dead-line. This is a problem we had throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you a specific question with regard to the answer you've given. You say it was asked that we control in full the so-called border. Why was the VJ not in a position to control in full the so-called border?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about borders in the standard meaning of the term, the military never controlled the entire borderline, only the stretches between official border crossings. At the official border crossings, there was the police as well as customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the incident that is being referred to here, that being the incident at the Batina bridge, based on what you've just said is a fact that that was a bridge something that affected jurisdiction of the VJ with regard to being able to control that area or not? And I'm assuming in my question that a bridge is an area can be used to cross a border.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. One cannot answer that question without being familiar with the situation in the FRY and the region as a whole, generally speaking. When the situation in the FRY is in question, the VJ had numerous problems because political authorities, and I might need to mention a particular name, and that is Slobodan Milosevic, had not only their official channels but also unofficial channels of conditionally speaking running the country and the administration. If I become even more specific, I would dare say that the military was not Milosevic's pet, quite the contrary. To say the least, he didn't like it and I believe he even hated it. And the same applied to the former JNA. He was much more in favour of the police and different other, I'd say, para-military organisations that he issued tasks to, or at least he turned a blind eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might interject now. Irrespective of Milosevic's position with regard to the VJ, were you aware of there being any laws that dealt with crossing state borders and movement in the border areas that directly affected the VJ's ability to control a border crossing such as the bridge at Batina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of what I have said in terms of the existing relationships is something I need to reiterate. What laws there existed at the time applied to what may and may not have been the border is something I can't say. I can only speak about facts and what the situation was in the field. That situation was not favourable to the army as an organised --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vuksic, both His Honour and I are suggest that you stop for the moment because you are not responding to the question that I've asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, the question is simply this: Was there anything, either in law or in fact, that prevented the VJ from controlling the border post if there was one on the bridge Batina? Your answer is, yes, there was something that could prevent it from controlling; no, there was nothing that could prevent us, or I don't know. It's a very simple question, Mr. Vuksic, please let us try to stay focused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I cannot answer that question in a brief way with a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's see if I can be of some assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have up on the screen D204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Guy-Smith, what do you want to do with 27D?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have that admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D357. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are most welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that would be tab number 35 in your binder. 35, sir. Don't look at the screen, look at your binder. Look at tab number 35.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And focusing your attention on paragraph 2, which discusses Article 48 of the Law on Crossing the State Border and Movement in the Border Area, are you aware of that being a law with regard to the jurisdiction of the various organisations at the FRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of who controlled the movement in stay of persons in the border area inside populated places in border crossings, can you tell the Chamber who had the jurisdiction to control those areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, any official border crossings were controlled by the police and customs. The Army of Yugoslavia was tasked with controlling areas outside designated border crossings, that is to say, the areas in between the different border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I do believe this has been previously admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, you said it is D204.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification. The document was marked for identification at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I maintain the position. I'm not moving it in at this point obviously. There's some translation issues that I think that may exist with it. So let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that I'm not sure whether I understand the answer to be consistent with the letter, with the document. The document seems to be saying it is -- that paragraph 2 that you referred to seems to be tasking the army units to look after the borders and not the police as I suspect was the answer from the witness. As I said, any official border crossings were controlled by the police and customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right, and if you look at the -- at this document it says that the border army unit shall secure the state border and control the movement and stay of persons in the border area, and then it's qualified specifically, outside populated places in border crossings. So the question is within populated places and border crossings, who had the jurisdiction, because this deals with an area that is outside of populated places and border, crossings, and it's specific in that regard. That's what I was driving at, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago when we were discussing the incident you said that -- and now if you could turn to tab 8 in your binder. I'd like you to take a look at this which is 26 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me double-check something, Your Honour, I seem to be calling these up in a wrong fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 65 ter 26D. 65 ter 26D, which is going to be, I believe, tab 13 in your binder. I'm sorry, tab 8 in your binder. Logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you're there. You're there. I can see it from here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. This is a -- are you familiar with this letter? This is a letter that was written by General Perisic to President Lilic. If you are familiar with the letter, fine; if not, so be it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, very good. Were you aware of any discussion with regard to the Batina bridge incident about a group of armed individuals who belonged to Deputy Raznjatovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And from whence did you obtain that information concerning this group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time -- at the time in Sector East in one of the Serb populated sectors that were under the protection of the UN forces, the liaison between the forces deployed there, i.e., the Russian and Belgian Battalions, there were two or three liaison officers stationed there permanently who had come from the administration that I headed. Their task was not to monitor this or similar events, but it was inevitable that they become aware of such incidents either immediately as they happened or subsequently, and it was those officers who informed me about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how this incident was ultimately --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how this incident was ultimately resolved internally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough. In 1993, did you have conversations with General Perisic concerning the importance of involving other world leaders in discussions about peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another document and see whether or not you recognise the document, or in the alternative recognise the incident that is being discussed in that document. And if we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you have it, what do you want to do with 26D?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to have it admitted, but I don't know whether there would be any objection, and I think there may be some foundational issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then at that point I can't move it for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't move it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can't move for its admission because I have a foundational problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you want to withdraw it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'll withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Well, I'd like to admit it, I mean, if you wish to have it admitted, but I don't think Mr. Thomas would agree nor would the Chamber. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could take a look in your binder at tab number 19, that would be 65 ter 32D. This is a letter that's written on the 17th of December, 1993. The first question is, are you familiar with the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 17th of December or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The letter of the 17th of December, yes. Letter written by General Perisic to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never seen this letter before. I mean at the time it was written. This is the first time that I'm seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of Mr. Milosevic receiving a letter from General Perisic concerning the importance of meeting with Boris Yeltsin and President Bill Clinton concerning proposals for the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to suspect that he didn't receive this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question is, my question is, are you aware of efforts made by General Perisic to have President Milosevic engage in this particular behaviour which is to meet with Mr. Yeltsin and Clinton concerning the views of how to reach a peaceful resolution of the crisis?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that on several occasions in different ways and in different places and on different occasions we considered what else the Yugoslav Army had do in order to persuade and convince the political leadership to effect or find as soon as possible and at any cost a political solution to the existing problems and to the conflicts that were in progress. I believe that this letter was written precisely with that intention in mind, although if somebody asked me at that time, or if I had seen this letter I would have said that this letter was overly optimistic, and that the recipients might construe this as something that shouldn't concern the Chief of General Staff who was not supposed to interfere with the highest level political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You mentioned that you know that on several occasions in different ways and in different places we considered what else Yugoslav Army had to do. In 1993, can you explain to the Chamber what meetings you had with General Perisic or other members of the VJ with this particular issue in mind, that issue being how to persuade the political leadership to find as soon as possible at any cost a solution to the problems?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that in 1993 I had meetings that were primarily aimed at resolving these issues because it was only in August of 1993 that General Perisic became Chief of General Staff of the VJ. I know that he was very busy, that he found it hard to finish his working day because he had so much to do, but one should understand that all the discussions and activities carried out in that respect were somehow overshadowed by the question of what to do in order to bring the developments in Yugoslavia to an end and to get back to normal life in a way for all the people and all the citizens and all ethnicities in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we go any further I'd move for its admission. I think that we've established a relationship between the witness and the document pursuant to the guide-line 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D358. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn our attention to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn our attention to a meeting in which you wrote a report, and if you could at this point look at tab number 21 in your binder, which is 65 ter 1061D, as in David. Have you had an opportunity to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I signed this document, I am familiar with this document, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in this document, there are a number of different matters that are being discussed between General Perisic and Commander Cot. First of all, there's an issue, paragraph 1, that deals with problems around the border between FRY and Macedonia, which was raised by General Thomson of UNPROFOR. Can you tell us what you recall with regard to those particular issues, the border issues between FRY and Macedonia that were raised by General Thomson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't the paragraph self-explanatory about that, that the paragraph says but he was unable to say what these problems were or why they occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, dealing with -- Mr. Vuksic said on occasion he has more to say, which is the reason I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he is the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'm well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You think he may have more information --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He may, he may not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He may have more information than he had then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that I was very much involved in following these problems and that I invested all my powers and efforts in the job that I was doing in order to avoid the creation of another hotbed or crisis spot between the FRY and Macedonia since our army had withdrawn from Macedonia in a peaceful way without any incidents whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. With regard to paragraph 2, 3, and 4, there is a discussion concerning violation of air-space by UN helicopters. Now, I know what you say here in the document, but what was the problem with the violation of air-space at that point in time? Why would that be a problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I can explain this in more clear way if I speak about UNPREDEP which is one of the first missions of that kind undertaken by the UN by deploying a peacekeeping contingent whose task was to prevent the occurrence of any incidents along the so-called never clearly established border line between the FRY and Macedonia. Due to that, these forces did not have clear tasks that they had, nor was it known where the actual border was between the FRY and the already independent former Yugoslavia or Republic of Macedonia. Whether this should be treated as coinciding with the former administrative border from the former Yugoslavia or whether it is something new that has to be determined and agreed upon. Another problem was that the international community believed that Macedonia as it was and its armed forces as they were at the time was incapable of controlling the border with the FRY itself. In my opinion, that was a rather arbitrary and unilateral opinion because it implied that somebody would resort to causing incidents, and it was difficult to accept this kind of attitude. We in the Yugoslav Army believed that regardless of that we should maintain good relations with these forces deployed in Macedonia. The incidents that took place were most often the ones that were anticipated. And it was really difficult to establish --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not anticipated, but supposed incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your report you indicate that General Cot said that he understood our position that the violations were not intentional and he would take the appropriate steps. Do you know whether or not any appropriate steps were taken or what was done to remedy the situation so that there would not be any further difficulties in this regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can express my satisfaction with what was done. We took the promise made by General Cot very seriously and on our part we undertook serious measures. Very soon, General Perisic authorised his deputy, General Kovacevic, to consider together with me, the most efficient way of dealing with the situation. In the meetings held with UNPREDEP representatives, which is United Nations preventative forces, we reached a conclusion that the best way and the best approach would be that we maintain permanent communication, that we discuss problems, that we meet and that none of those so-called incidents should be given undue prominence until it was established whether it actually happened or not. We knew that all this was unintentional and that General Perisic made that clear to General Cot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If we could turn to paragraph 3 of the document, sir. Now, paragraph 3 discusses something that we have been already having some discussion about, and that regards the transport of the weapons and equipment of NordBat, and what I'd like to focus on is the second full paragraph under paragraph 3, which starts with the words "General Perisic said..." I'll give you a chance to read that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, here you indicate that "General Perisic said that our relationship with the Army of Republika Srpska is not" - in my translation says - "commanding, and that all problems should be resolved in co-operation with RS authorities and with their approval. Such problems could have been avoided if they," could you tell us who the "they" is that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would kindly ask this translation to be corrected. I'm going to tell you what was it that I exactly wrote and I said that General Perisic indicated that our relations with the Army of Republika Srpska was not the one that involved issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, that meant that we couldn't order them anything and that we didn't wish to do so. We thought that all the problems should be resolved with the authorities of Republika Srpska and with their consent, and we had it in mind what we had already told to the UN organs because we thought that they should have acquired the approval of Republika Srpska prior to sending the weapons to the territory of the FRY and then to ask us to permit this weapons to be transferred to the territory of Republika Srpska. So that was one of the problems that featured constantly in our relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "featured constantly in our relations," who are you referring to in terms of "in our relations?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say that, I mean all of the international players and representatives regardless of whether they came from New York, Washington, Brussels, or any other countries, the OSCE, or if they were members or representatives of any of the UN missions and forces. There was always the expectation and sometimes even the declaration that General Mladic would do whatever he was told to do by the VJ or specifically Chief of Staff. That was by no means true and the assumption itself was entirely erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to the section number 2 of this same document, those issues deal with Pancevo barracks, which I think we've discussed previously, and in that you also mention in paragraph, that would be paragraph 2 in section 2, you mention the barracks in Zemin. Could you tell us whether or not ultimately the agreement that was reached had UNPROFOR forces leaving the barracks in Pancevo and moving to the barracks in Zemin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point it suffices to simply repeat what is written here --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's no need to do that. If it's simply written there, that takes care of the issue, then we can rely on what has been written there, and I thank you, Mr. Vuksic, for your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move this document's admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D359. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, one of the things that you've discussed with us was that you had set up an administration after your proposal to General Perisic that dealt both with international organisations as well as foreign military attaches, and I'd like to dwell on that for a moment in terms of 1993. And are you aware of a discussion that was had in November of 1993 between the Italian intelligence service and members of the VJ in Italy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was aware of those meetings taking place. I was not, however, in a position to read any reports, documents to do with that. Nevertheless, I am aware of the persons holding those posts at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who were those persons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Branko Cagic [phoen], Major-General Branko Cagic who was at the time the chief of the intelligence administration, and Colonel Petar Stojic who was chief of the department for -- that liaising with foreign military representatives, which as you said at a later stage became part of this joint administration for international military co-operation, to put it as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are you aware of the position of the Italian government with regard to working or co-operating with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Italy's position in general was the same as over the preceding years. They were our neighbours, and I would put it this way. I think this is the most acceptable way of putting it. They felt this way about it. There's something going on in our neighbourhood that is quite unpleasant and constitutes a threat to peace and security. Italy has an interest in this. Italy wishes to lend a hand in terms of doing anything that is reasonable in order to normalise the situation and put an end to the crisis. At the time the Italians also told us as follows: As far as Serbia or the FRY or the Serbian people are concerned, we have no bone of contention with you. I'm talking about the earlier period. Nevertheless, if Yugoslavia breaks up and Croatia becomes independent, the situation changes. They would normally leave it at that. We had no interest in meddling in the affairs of Italy and this potentially independent Croatia, and they for their part did not have any particular interest in making it clear to us what this bone of contention might be. It wasn't clear at the time or for that matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might ask you to go to tab 11 in your binder, which would be 65 ter 521D. And this is a report dated 25 December 1993, which was written by the individuals whom you've just mentioned. And I'd like to refer -- I'd like to refer your attention, if I could, to the following passage which is: "In open talks that were held in a friendly atmosphere, General Puchi asked us to pass on the following message to the president of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic: 1, the Italian government is aware that the FRY of Yugoslavia or Serbia is the basic factor of stability in the Balkans. Being conscious of the fact that frequent mistakes were made when dealing with Serbia and Montenegro and that the sanctions against the FRY of Yugoslavia have had a counter-productive affect (he mentioned that their effectiveness was only around 15 to 20 per cent) at the international level Italy will urge to have them reduced and gradually cancelled. In order to be able to do so, it needs the help of S. Milosevic, who is regarded by the Italians as the only figure of decisive influence in finding a solution to the Yugoslav crisis. They therefore believe that President Milosevic of the Republic of Serbia should do his utmost to persuade the Bosnian Serbs to agree to the French German proposal for the solution of the crisis in the territory of the former BH, and if an agreement on cessation of hostilities is still not reached after that, blame should be placed on those who are blocking it. With regard to this, he expressed the readiness of Italy and the European Union to apply pressure on Izetbegovic." Now, my first question is with regard to the information that is contained within this paragraph. Is this information that you were privy to, and by that I mean that the subject matter of what is being discussed are matters that you discussed either with these gentlemen or with others concerning the position of Italy at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen the document by this time. Nevertheless, given the nature of my work I was aware of these conversations. To some extent, I knew what the gist of those contacts was. And the same applies to Italy's position regarding the sanctions, or to put it that way penalizing Serbia and Montenegro. I'm asking myself whether General Puchi really believed that the sanctions achieved a 15 to 20 per cent success rate in terms of the damage done to the economy and living conditions in the FRY. I wonder if he really believed that the success rate in terms of furthering the peace process was really 15 per cent. As far as the economy and the general situation in Yugoslavia, I think the success rate of the sanctions was actually closer to 100 per cent, which is something that I experienced myself to my own detriment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
