utterances.text: I understand. Let me ask you this: With regard to the agreement to the French German proposal for the solution of the crisis, do you know which proposal he is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I would perhaps have an a assumption about that, but it would be purely speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If we could turn to paragraph 5 of the same document, which deals with the issue of NATO as being considered a military option, and my question to you is with regard to NATO being considered as a military option in 1993, was that a matter that you discussed with any of your contemporaries who were in foreign services, by that I mean representing any of the NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I had to raise this unpleasant topic more than once with a number of different people from different countries, different international organisations, representatives of the UN. On one occasion I had the assignment of appearing at press conference to explain what an armed intervention by NATO would mean, and that the destruction of bridges over the Drina would be interpreted as a direct attack on the FRY. If I had been aware of the broader context because back in 1992 it was with great satisfaction that I had read a piece written about that by the then chief of the joint General Staff of the armed forces of the USA General Pauly who stole the politicians thunder and asked the politicians five questions that they were to answer before ever tasking him with a NATO intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was glad to read that that honourable man had done just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer in that regard. Now, finally, turning to paragraph 4, it indicates the following: "The latest incidents in the territory the former Yugoslavia clearly show that this is a civil and religious war, and not Serbian aggression, and the constructive contributions by the Yugoslav leadership, especially S. Milosevic, have contributed to the Italian media having a far more objective approach to the Yugoslav crisis and writing increasingly favourably about Serbia and Montenegro." And with regard to the statement here about the Italian media having a far more objective approach to the Yugoslav crisis, can you tell us if you know whether or not, first of all, in your opinion there was a far more objective approach, and second of all, far more objective approach then who would that be? Are we discussing here media wars, are we discussing here -- if you know what is being discussed here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this paragraph, if I may, what was going on in some parts of the former Yugoslavia was not just a civilian war and a religious war, but also an ethnic war. At different points in time, different aspects would gain the upperhand in this conflict depending on the intensity of hatred in certain parts of the former country. As for Milosevic, of course that is a pure exaggeration and a form of encouragement. As for my opinion to the effect that there had been a turnaround in the press coverage, I think at this point in time the turnaround was not yet really so marked as to be considered an essential sea change. I don't think I can provide any particular details. Normally, the diplomatic representatives were the people who covered the media and wrote up reports about media coverage. I myself was not receiving any reports like that in my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D360. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I now wish to turn to 1994 specifically to discuss with you the first of what I will term the hostage incidents that occurred in 1994, in the spring of 1994. And my first question to you is, were you aware of there being an incident involving hostages that were taken, French citizens, in the spring of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that incident, which doesn't mean that I was officially informed. Rather, I was aware of this incident and I knew that the incident would not bring us any luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who took the hostages, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about 1994, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hostages, the same as those in 1995, were taken by the military, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the military that took these hostages, the VRS, do you know what efforts were made specifically, if any that is, specifically by General Perisic with regard to the release of those hostages in the spring of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To take representatives of the UN peacekeeping forces hostage, no matter whether you are actually happy with their work or not, no matter whether they were always right or not, was an utterly unreasonable decision. It was an attempt at vengeance and only served to exacerbate the crisis in terms of the relations between all the mediating players and all the peacekeeping players throughout the former Yugoslavia and particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know, once again, what efforts General Perisic made with regard to the release of those hostages. Obviously with the answer you've just given in mind, do you know what he did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many times before and after, General Perisic had a particularly significant and delicate role to play. He was supposed to carry out certain tasks that sometimes resemble the task of tilting at windmills which would not be entirely uncommon given the lie of the land in the country of Holland. He was supposed to explain to representatives of the VJ and General Ratko Mladic that there was something that they weren't doing right, that there was something that they should improve, particularly in terms of releasing those hostages. I do know, however, that neither General Perisic nor I were ever in a position to tell General Mladic or anyone else that they had done something wrong which would sometimes leave him in a situation in which he was unable to continue a reasonable discussion. We all started out by discussing facts, something happened, let's try and do something about trying to not cause any further harm, and that was precisely what General Perisic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, and I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, are you familiar with a gentleman whose name was Colonel Vialatte?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Vialatte.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber who this gentleman was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vialatte was an envoy from the defence ministry of the Republic of France serving in the FRY at the time I took over as head of the administration for liaising with international military representatives international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you took over, did you have occasion to meet with this gentleman and discuss matters of mutual interest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That was his first duty and my principal duty as well, whenever he had anything to share with me, or for that matter, whenever I had anything to share with him. When I say "anything to share," what I mean is our regular procedural duties that we performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what were your regular procedural duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and other officers serving in the administration were supposed to get in touch and talk with international military representatives as well as representatives of international organisations. We were supposed to cover any issues or problems that had to do with the VJ's relations with certain countries that these respective gentlemen represented, or indeed with the international organisations represented by these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the matter that we were discussing before the break, that being the hostages, did you have discussion with this gentleman concerning the hostages that were taken in the spring of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to add the following though: Colonel Vialatte in his capacity as an official representative of the armed forces of the Republic of France serving as an envoy in the FRY was not the first person or the most important person to discuss an issue like that. This was in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If you could go to your binder and go to tab number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 31D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document, and I was aware of the document at the time it was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is dated the 12th of April, 1994. It's to the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and it says "Colonel Vialatte, the Defence attache of the French embassy in Belgrade, expresses his respects to the Chief of the General Staff the Yugoslav Army and has the honour to attach this document a request for the release of four French people from the Pharmaciens Sans Frontieres humanitarian organisation who have been detained since 4 March 1995." First of all, I take it that the four people who are being referred to in this document are the individuals that we have been discussing before we brought this letter up; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a little question? Are we sure that 1995 is correct if this letter is written in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm reading what the -- I understand there may be a typo in the letter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We'll find out. Somehow or another we'll get to the date of this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next paragraph reads: "Colonel Vialatte understanding perfectly that those who are imprisoning the four French people are not subordinate to the," and I'm reading specific what I have in my translation here, "the NGS of the VJ." I don't know how it reads for you in your document, but could you tell us, please, after the words "are not subordinate to" who is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those who are imprisoning the French people. Do you want to know their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are not subordinate to the NGS, I'm assuming that's the General Staff of the VJ. As I understand that what this says is "Colonel Vialatte understands perfectly that those who are imprisoning are not subordinate to the General Staff of the VJ. " My understanding -- that's why I just want to make sure that I'm dealing with the General Staff of the VJ, first of all, because my translation reads NGS. I don't want to take any liberties here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the witness can tell us what NGS stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you do that, Mr. Vuksic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubt about this, this is the official abbreviation that stands for chief of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the statement here that those who are imprisoning the four French people, you had earlier mentioned that those individuals were being imprisoned by General Mladic. To your knowledge, is that -- are those the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I might be wrong, sir, but I recall the answer being the VRS, not General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies, if it was the VRS and not Mladic, let me -- I'll have it double-checked, but in either event whether it be Mladic or the VRS, people who were being imprisoned were being imprisoned by another, how shall I put this, another army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubt about this. They were being imprisoned by members of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The letter guess on to -- go ahead, I'm sorry if I interrupted you. Did I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The letter goes on to state: "He also feels assured that the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, in order to preserve the image of the Serbs who are traditionally respected for their valour and honour, will not neglect this opportunity to use his influence in order to bring this painful affair to a close, in the name of the traditional amity between Serbian and France, as is anticipated by all French people." Now, are you aware of whether or not General Perisic attempted to use his influence or used his influence with regard to this painful affair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic took steps that were in line with this beautifully composed letter, which I find very interesting. The four arrested members of Medecins Sans Frontieres were released, although, I don't know at what point in time. I called the letter interesting. If necessary, I can explain. If that's not required, then I'll abstain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, why don't you explain.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old-school French diplomacy used a particularly high level of distinguished communication when addressing others. Old-school French diplomats also tend to use careful phrasing and particularly elevated language. Secondly, Colonel Vialatte said in no uncertain terms he was aware of the fact that those holding the four men prisoners were not subordinated to the chief of the VJ General Staff. Thirdly, these four members of Medecins Sans Frontieres were no military persons. Therefore, it would have been logical for the health minister or whoever was the counter-part in France to address another sector or ministry within the FRY. This was, however, not the only situation in which Colonel Vialatte had broader powers when it came to certain specific assignments. Assignments which under normal circumstances would have exceeded his authority. I'm able to say based on my personal experience that this is something that is typical of the way the French work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. And I think I may have been -- I may have made a mistake with regard to the date of this incident. I believe this was the spring of 1995, not the spring of 1994. And just as you remember, do you recall which year it was? Because I may have led you astray in my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say. The letter states the 12th of April, 1994. The heading says the 6th of March, 1995. Of course, this is possibly a mistranslation, so the translator wrote 1995 instead of writing 1994. Nevertheless in this note that I signed, the note in which we invoked our of confidential number 5-15 dated the 13th of April, 1995, I am unable to ascertain what the correct date might be. Nevertheless, my comment would not change in any way regarding the substance of the letter. And the substance does not depend on whether this in fact occurred in 1994 or 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance would remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now going to move on to another document at this time. And we will not be introducing this document at this time until we get some more clarification about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could now move to your tab 5, which is 65 ter 352 which is in a document which is in English only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is dated August 8th, 1994. The subject matter -- yes, I'll start with the subject matter. The subject matter is "Perisic, UN commander talks solve 'delicate problems.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose 352 is a D document? Just a 352, 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been told. On our list, on the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The source of this document is Belgrade, domestic service and Serb Croatian 1421 GMT 8 August 1994, and the text reads as follows: "Belgrade 8 August, (Tanjug) Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and his aides today received French General Bertrand De Lapresle commander of UN Protection Force (UNPROFOR) in the former Yugoslavia, at the latter's request, the information service of the Yugoslav Army's General Staff announced today: 'Issues of importance for relations between UNPROFOR and the Yugoslav Army were aired during the frank talks, and it was stressed that some delicate problems were solved, thanks to the two sides' constructive approach. This refers particularly to the area bordering on the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, where an incident-prone situation has been considerably defused through mutual efforts by UNPROFOR and the Yugoslav Army. General Perisic and De Lapresle agreed that the Yugoslav Army has made a considerable contribution to the efforts to find a peaceful solution to the crisis in the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia,' a statement says." My question to you is, do you know what the delicate problems that were solved were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to reiterate that in my view, then as now, everything that was considered to be problematic in our relations is something I never truly believed were problems indeed. I can't tell you specifically what this problem would be, the one referred to here, but there was an issue, for example, when certain representatives of the VJ arrested --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there since you say, "I can't tell you specifically what this problem would be," it's one referred to here, further on in this particular document it says: "Where an incident-prone situation has been considerably diffused through mutual efforts by UNPROFOR and the Yugoslav Army." Are you in a position to tell us what the incident-prone situation which was considerably diffused was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier on when I referred to the problems between the FRY and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, as some called it, was in the vein of recognising that there were general problems in existence because there were no internationally recognised legal borders. In terms of resolving such problems we decided to view the administrative border as the border that was to be respected by both sides, the FRY and VJ on one side, and the Macedonian authorities as well as the prevention mission of the UN and Macedonia on the other. This was viewed as our great contribution, and I believe that indeed it was an act of goodwill on our part. We and the army believed it needed to be done immediately, however, representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and of the interior dragged their feet, as usual. Usually, the army was the more flexible body which perhaps had a more politically sober view of the situation than the two bodies I just referred to. I believe this incident was the one when a representative of the peacekeeping forces who was actually a US Army member, in view of our border authorities, who were obviously not favourably disposed towards representatives of the US, arrested him, stating that he crossed over into the territory of the FRY. When something like that happens it is reported the world over and is deemed a significant issue, especially if it involved a member of the US armed forces. As for the FRY, we conducted our own investigation immediately and the issue of whether we would release him or not was never seriously considered, of course. However, our interior organs were of a slightly different view because the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ or of any army is not the sole person to resolve such matters. That is why this issue lasted a couple of days longer than necessary. I believe that General De Lapresle believed that such a development deserved to figure in his report, although I cannot say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the development that figured, if I understand you, your testimony, is that he and General Perisic worked out some agreement for the release of this particular American soldier, and if that's wrong, please do tell me that I'm not correct in my understanding.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was quite like that, I would be more prone to say that General Perisic's explanation during his conversations with General De Lapresle was a convincing one and that General De Lapresle on that occasion as well as on many other occasions before and after that was able to say that there were no problems in dealing with the VJ when current issues needed to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D361. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I now want to turn your attention to military co-operation between FRY and the Republic of Hungary. And I'd like to start off by asking you, were you aware of there being any discussions, conferences, or contacts between FRY, the military of FRY and the military of Hungary with regard to co-operation at any point in time? You know what, I won't put it that way. During 1994, I'll make it more specific, although I know I'm taking a bit of a lead in here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the nature of my work I had to be informed of such developments because this went through the Hungarian military representative to the FRY with whom I co-operated, as well as through the military envoy of the FRY to Hungary. Both of them in turn had to be informed immediately irrespective of the channels through which a specific letter, draft agreement, or any such document arrived. This was the gentleman's agreement we had and in diplomacy at that level, it would have been seen as something very unfavourable if one side omitted to inform the representative of another country. It would be viewed as an underestimation of the importance of that person's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. If you could do us the kindness and turn to tab 16 in your binder, which would be 65 ter 28D?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there are two associated documents with it, Mr. Registrar, which I'll be calling up in sequential order which are 29 and 30, so you know, but we'll deal with them obviously one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated the 17th of October, 1994. What I'd like to do is immediately direct your attention to the bottom of the document where it indicates the distribution list in the bottom, to whom this document was distributed to. And is this in line with what you just told us, and by that I mean, I note that it says VJGS administration for relations with foreign military representatives and international organisations. That would have been your bailiwick?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And looking at the document itself, Mr. Vuksic, the document is discussing, as I understand it, a draft of an agreement on military co-operation between the RV and PVO of the armed forces of the Republic of Hungary and FRY in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is have this document admitted at this time and then move on to the next document so that we can discuss them all in a collective matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence, May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D362. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if we could have the next document up. That would be tab number 17 in your binder, sir. That would be 65 ter 29D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which, as I understand it, is the cover letter to the actual agreement on the military co-operation between the RV PVO of the Army of Republic of Hungary and the FRY, which was referred to in the previously admitted exhibit. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... admission. Thank you. I move for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D364 -- pardon me, 363. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the next document would be found at tab number 18, which would be sequentially 65 ter 30D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is entitled "Agreement on Military Co-Operation in the Areas of the RV and the PVO Contracted Between the Government of the Republic of Hungary and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And I ask you the same question. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the agreement on military co-operation between the two parties, do you know whether or not this agreement was reached in 1994 or not, and I direct your attention to the end of the document which would be Article 8, section 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was it an actual agreement entered into between Hungary and FRY in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for the simple reason that I need to tell the truth. However, I'd like to point out that it may not be so important, the fact whether it was signed and when because it was limited by Article 8.3, you pointed out because of the UN Resolution number 757. It is also important to note that such discussions were held and that it was a topical issue at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you've a actually focused on the very point of my inquiry, which is considering UN Resolution number 757, do you know what that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot memorise the contents of every resolution. In any case, this particular resolution had to do with sanctions and the isolation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in certain aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand and hopefully you can be of some help here is considering the work that you were doing in 1994 was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under sanctions, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately I recall that very well. The sanctions were introduced against the FRY in 1992 and by way of further resolutions and decisions, they were strengthened. I cannot tell you exactly when the stringency was at its highest though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's okay, because my question relates in another fashion. Can you explain to the Chamber in light of the presence of these sanctions, if you know, how you were going about engaging in discussions for military co-operations with other nation states?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will start replying by providing a remark which may seem a bit philosophical, but I believe the Chamber is sufficiently tolerant to hear me out. All matters in this world are relative, if not sooner than later, as was proven by the theory of relativity. When I say this, I'm trying to point out that it was very difficult to implement everything that was on paper at the time by way of sanctions levelled against us. In parallel with those papers and the situation the FRY was put in, there were efforts running to try and ease that to make it more relative so as to give certain encouragement to the people of Yugoslavia and its authorities in order to indicate that we were not completely forgotten and rejected, and that once conditions are created for it, we were to become a normal country co-operating with others again. This particularly had to do with the Army of Yugoslavia, which was supposed to have been isolated the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's where I'd like if you could, please, if you could focus because as we understand it and we've heard a fair amount of testimony concerning sanctions that were blocking in relatively strong terms, a contact, a certain military contact with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia how these kinds of agreements -- discussions about these agreements could be taking place during the period of time these sanctions were imposed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that. I can only say that I was happy it was taking place at the time. When I think about it now I believe that despite everything, somebody somewhere said that occasionally a blind eye needed to be turned and that the country that was isolated in such a way still deserved to be accorded contacts and discussions. I have lots of proof for that and I know that General Perisic at his position of the chief of the General Staff during those years visited Romania and Austria more than once as well as Hungary. I don't know whether it was because the Hungarians, Romanians, or Austrians were particularly founding of us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for a moment. You said that you know that General Perisic in his position as chief of the General Staff visited Romania, Austria, and more than once as well as Hungary. With regard to Romania, do you know what the nature of those visits were apart from the fact that he was visiting Romania in his official capacity as Chief of the General Staff of the VJ? Do you know what the subject matter at hand was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any such visit at that level receives relevant military significance and plays an important role in the relations of two countries. When he visited Romania, I was a member of the delegation, or one of them, and if I hadn't known any better, I would have said that there were no sanctions in place. Our relations were such as would otherwise have been exhibited among friends at that level without any hedges whatsoever basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed any topic that was of mutual interest at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand you discussed any topic, I'm wondering if you can be specific in that regard. If you can that's fine, if you can't that's fine as well, which is what kinds of topics were discussed at that time when you were part of the delegation that went to Romania in a military official capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you a lot about that but I don't want to waste your time. I can say very clearly that both the Romanians and the Hungarians spoke a lot about their intentions and about how they were paving a way for the both countries to become NATO members. They told us what they were doing, that didn't conceal the fact that that was a more important task for them than their combat readiness, and we were able to see for ourselves on the spot that that was true. They told us that once the situation has normalised, they were convinced that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would become a member of the partnership for peace and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. You've mentioned a new element which is the partnership for peace. Could you please describe for the Chamber what the partnership for peace was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partnership for peace was an initiative adopted at a NATO meeting in Brussels held at the level of the heads of states or governments of NATO countries. I think it took place in January, I think 1994 or 1995. It was conceived as a process of preparations for certain countries, eastern countries, former communist countries that were supposed to demonstrate, and some of them did so, a desire to become NATO countries. I don't think there's any need for me to enumerate these countries but I'll do it anyway, those were Poland, Romania, Czechoslovakia or rather the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Bulgaria, et cetera, who after a certain period of time indeed became NATO members. That was a programme of co-operation in the area of approximately 2.000 issues or rather a list of issues that was never closed. I followed these problems and NATO members were open for discussion of any issue that a potential candidate for NATO membership would raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the partnership for peace initiative, and maybe moving somewhat forward in time, could you tell us, if you know, what General Perisic's position was with regard to FRY becoming involved in the partnership for peace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of General Perisic vis-a-vis the partnership for peace as the initiative that merited great attention was very positive. He was interested in becoming familiarised with it and he wanted to be briefed about it. He also wanted the competent organs to keep following this with due care and that is what actually happened in the period that followed, at least as far as the Yugoslav Army was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had mentioned that among other places that General Perisic had visited Hungary in his official capacity, and I would like you at this time, if you could, go to your binder and if you could go to your tab, that would be tab number, I believe it's 13. That would be 65 ter 550D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm reminded by Mr. Mair that I may have neglected in moving the previous exhibit, 65 ter 30D, into evidence and I would ask that it occurs at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 30D is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D364. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved in setting this meeting up with a Chief of Staff of the Hungarian army, Lieutenant-General Sandor Nemeth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was by virtue of my official capacity which meant that all the preparations that were carried out through the Hungarian envoy in Belgrade was implemented through my administration, but I was not a member of the delegation which could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. I'd like to go down to what would be the fourth paragraph which starts off with the following: "The Chief of General Staff of the Hungarian army, Sandor Nemeth, then if he with could refer ourselves to the second sentence, which says: "Relations between our armies were free from obstructions before the embargo, but he pointed out the need to find possibilities for co-operation even under the certainly limited circumstances." I believe he that is being referred to here is chief of the General Staff of the Hungarian army, Sandor Nemeth. Now, were you aware of this particular view that even under the currently limited circumstances that there was a need to find co-operation, possibilities for co-operation between your army and the Hungarian army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this actually confirms what I already said and explained in broader terms, so one should perceive this in this context, the agreement between the two countries in the area of air force and anti-aircraft defence mentioned earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Continuing on in this particular document, there is -- it would be on my page 2, I don't know if it correlates that way for you. There is a paragraph that starts with the language "they" which I believe is referring once again to the Hungarian army "see the partnership for peace as the west's response to the wish of so many so-called 'new democracies' to join NATO immediately" -- it's the sixth paragraph down in B/C/S I'm informed by Mr. Zorko, thank you. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "And awaited response to this decision until economically, technically and technologically ready to join. It is a framework to improve the situation by getting to know the method, process, and system of training and participation in bilateral or multilateral exercises." And just stopping right there. Could you explain to the Chamber what bilateral and multilateral exercises are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can if necessary. Generally speaking there are bilateral and multilateral relations between countries, alliances, and some other entities, not only in the military, but in other spheres as well. Bilateral co-operation implies co-operation between two countries. It could be in the area of military, which would involve then co-operation of armed forces of two countries. Since NATO is a multilateral international organisation, there was a possibility for two NATO member countries to co-operate on a bilateral basis provided a decision to that effect is taken and provided it is accepted by the Brussel. There was also a possibility for a NATO member country to enter into bilateral co-operation with a country that aspires to become a NATO member, again provided this is agreed by the NATO organs and the potential NATO candidate. This even applied to military exercises because that is the most delicate mode of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In 1994 was the VJ involved in any military exercises with any other militaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, military exercises were out of the question. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not only in isolation but pursuant to Resolution 713 of the UN, the territory of the former Yugoslavia was a no zone for delivery of any weapons or equipment. This resolution was passed in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you. The document goes on to indicate that they would like a verbal agreement on co-operation in the space to continuing functioning as it had been agreed and for it to be officially verified in writing. They propose that two ministers sign a framework agreement on co-operation. I'm sorry, they propose that the two ministers sign a framework agreement on co-operation. Which two ministers are being referred to there, if you know, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I read it here in front of me, it says, "It has been proposed for the two ministers to conclude a framework agreement on co-operation." That means that the two ministers of defence were supposed to draft a framework agreement on specific modes of co-operations that would be implemented or would come in force immediately after the lifting of the sanctions imposed against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In other words, the sanctions imposed under the Resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand, thank you. Continuing in that paragraph it says: "They believe they cannot arbitrate in the conflict in the territory of the former SFRY but think they can have an indirect influence in normalising relations." I'd like to focus your attention to this issue of influence on normalising relations. What would be the indirect influence they could have, if you know, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this on the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It may well be, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that particular portion, but I do understand very well what this is all about. Hungary had very strong reasons even ethical reasons to initiate co-operation with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia including military co-operation given that at the beginning of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia the Croatian para-military formations were supplied via Hungary with an enormous amount of weapons and ammunition. In order to promote co-operation, they thought that they could influence now the behaviour of Croatia as an independent state with a view to normalising relations with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to direct your attention in B/C/S to page 2, it would be the eighth paragraph down which would be discussing the sentence that I just indicated, "They believe they cannot arbitrate the conflict in the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but they think they could have an indirect influence on normalising relations." I just want to know if you can see that in the text that you are reading?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say this they thought they could influence the behaviour of Croatia, how -- if you know, how does -- would they go about engaging in that influence of that behaviour? What would they do, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that this could have been done, first of all, at the government level, and how that would have been done concretely depended on what they wanted to achieve. As an illustration I can mention that recently the president of the Republic of Hungary offered his good offices in order to establish a contact between the president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Boris Talic, and the new elected president of the Republic of Croatia, Ivo Josipovic given that a few months ago these relations during the pre-election campaign in Croatia were sort of sore. These offer for good offices could be public but also as diplomats would say could be implemented behind closed doors, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I would now like to go to the next paragraph because something that you just told us seems to strike me as curious strange. You indicated that FRY was not in a position to engage in military exercises, you just told us that. As I read this next paragraph, I'd like you to give us some help here. The paragraph says: "Since two vessels from their river fleet," I take it that would be the Hungarian army's or Hungarian's river fleet, "are to take part in a joint exercise in Romania ..." Now, the language here "joint exercise," would that be a military exercise that Hungary and Romania would be exercising in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, minor correction for the sake of clarity, Hungary doesn't have a fleet. A fleet usually implies a navy. This is a flotilla which is of great significance for our soldiers but it's not significant in this particular instance. This was a joint exercise between Hungary and Romania. The Hungarian ships were to sail down the Danube and cross the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Here is where I'm having some difficulty in understanding the answer that you've given. You've told us that FRY was prohibited from engaging in military exercises. And you've indicated to us that there was an embargo in place. And as I understand this, what is being requested here by the Hungarian military because they wish to engage in a military exercise with Romania, is they are requesting assistance in allowing passage of them along the Danube through the country of FRY. Then it says primarily in providing maintenance and service. But wouldn't that be a violation of the embargo for FRY to allow any kind of military vessel to pass through? Wouldn't that be as one would say wrong in terms of the embargo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, formally speaking, yes, but as I said after Einstein's theory, everything is relative in this world. So perhaps if a decision is taken somewhere to certain level for something to be acceptable and if we say that means justify the end, one can act accordingly. Of course, Hungary didn't do that without seeking approval from certain authorities that supervised or controlled the embargo, NATO was involved in that, but not on the Danube. They did that in the Mediterranean and on the Adriatic Sea. I think this is fully in line with what we already said a few times is that all of this was relative. One can say that the Yugoslav Army who was asked to allow not only passage but also the repair and servicing and this is an unfinished sentence, it says that in case of need, they would provide repair services for the voyage of these vessels, but certain things could have happened that would necessitate the repair of such vessels in the territory of Yugoslavia, that is to say on the river Danube. So that was an additional element that would help us to agree on what we discussed earlier and that is certain goodwill measures that were granted to certain countries in order to avoid Yugoslavia being completely and hopelessly isolated and discarded by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Continuing with this particular document, it discusses with the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslavia army stated. Then it says: "Conclusion and assessment of the visit: The invitation and overall visit were assessed as a well intentioned gesture by the new leadership in the Hungarian army and an initial initiative which should be followed by co-operation on specific tasks. The VJ chief of the General Staff extended an invitation to the Hungarian army delegation for an official return visit to the FRY." To your knowledge was on official return visit to the FRY made by the Hungarian army delegation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at this juncture whether this visit took place or not. It may have happened later on after I ceased to be head of that administration, but this passage confirms the view of the chief the General Staff that it was a gesture of goodwill on the part of the new leadership of Hungary and the state of Hungary itself. The extension of an invitation for return visit --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The document also indicates: "The overall impression is that there is no danger of a threat to the FRY from the Hungarian army." I'm trying to understand, is that something that was of importance in these kinds of reports is a threat assessment of neighbouring or close countries to the FRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These kinds of visits at the level of chiefs of General Staffs cannot be effected or carried out without mentioning this particular aspect, that is to say whether in any way could anyone predict that there was direct danger or threat to the security by either country to the other country. This language confirms that General Perisic was convinced of that himself, and this should have served the political leadership in their efforts towards developing better relations between the two countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I move for the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One final question and you can give us a yes or no answer to this question, if possible, which is, do you recall there being a joint air meeting, and by that I mean in which airplanes and air force were flown from France, Russia, Italy, and Greece? It's not in that document, sir. Mr. Vuksic, it's not in the document, sir. Do you recall there being a joint military meeting in which air forces from the countries that I've just mentioned, France, Russia, Italy, and Greece, occurred during the time of the embargo in the territory of FRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was trying to do it quickly, so I'll pick it up tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, once again I remind you that you are not supposed to discuss the case with anybody until you are excused from further testifying. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow morning at 9.00 same Courtroom II. Court adjourned.
